originality.rationale: The relevant prior result is not just the definition of k-Abelian equivalence. Karhumäki, Puzynina, Rao and Whiteland (arXiv:1605.03319, 2016) give the exact switch-generation theorem and a general singleton characterization by uniqueness of (k−1)-factor returns. The frozen ambiguity switch is exactly their switch at k=2. In the double-occurrence setting every possible switch is of the form a1<b1<a2<b2: a shared middle index would require a third occurrence, and equality of the two endpoint labels is likewise impossible. In a FIFO mountain encoding the only such pairs are within BB, and both returns are identical. In a nonmountain excursion the first and last letters of the initial ascent have distinct returns because a new letter is opened between their respective second occurrences. Thus the frozen singleton classification is a direct specialization of the prior singleton criterion plus the elementary FIFO/Dyck characterization; the resulting composition count is already indexed under the equivalent block representation. No publication-priority inference is made from a different same-day record.
residual_risks: The exact FIFO/Dyck wording was not found printed in the primary article; the verdict rests on the demonstrated specialization, not on that wording or a search miss. The exact sequential order of the same-day catalog findings is unknown.

value.rationale: The reconstruction question is natural and the mountain description is a useful concise explanation. But as a separate exact finding, the boundary here is a routine application of the general singleton theorem to two occurrences with FIFO order. Once the two returns are compared, the induced path, mountain blocks and enumerated compositions follow from the same first-descent case, and the count is a known block count. No further nontrivial reconstruction invariant or quantitative fiber theorem is established.
residual_risks: This assesses additional scientific value as a distinct finding, not the expository usefulness of the graph and Dyck path descriptions.
